episodes.title: The man who fought napster is now fighting AI
episodes.about: Nilay Patel talks with Mitch Glazier, who was a young RIAA lawyer during the Napster lawsuits and now leads the music industry's fight over AI. They cover the major labels' proposed rules to keep AI slop off the charts, reporting that Suno snatched songs from YouTube, Genius, and Deezer, and the Warner Music-Suno and Universal Music-Udio deals that settled lawsuits - and why Glazier says fighting AI firms is more fun than suing Napster users.
episodes.why: Out today: the RIAA lawyer from the Napster cases now runs the labels' AI fight - chart rules for AI slop, scraped-song training, and the Suno and Udio settlements in one conversation.

episodes.title: Agentic Video Is Real and Here’s What You Should Try
episodes.about: AI agents are making it possible to edit, animate, and produce videos simply by describing what you want. NLW explores what changed and how to put it to work - from meeting highlights and concept demos to animated business updates and customer education videos that update themselves. Plus, three levels for getting started, from editing existing recordings to building recurring video workflows.
episodes.why: Agents can now edit, animate, and produce a whole video from a description; NLW sorts what actually works into three levels, from cutting recordings to self-updating customer videos.

episodes.title: Why PMs are suddenly valuable again | Tulsee Doshi (Head of Product, Gemini)
episodes.about: Tulsee Doshi is head of product for Google's frontier AI models, including Gemini and the multimodal models Nano Banana, Genie, Veo, and Lyria. She and Lenny Rachitsky discuss what product managers actually do inside a frontier AI lab, why model development is not just engineering, Google's full-stack strategy, her 60-20-20 framework for balancing what works now against what's almost working, and how to write your first eval.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Lenny's Podcast is Lenny Rachitsky's product-management show, new here: Gemini's head of product on what PMs do inside a frontier lab and how evals get written.

episodes.title: The Equal Talent Conundrum
episodes.about: Two people can have equally promising business ideas and very different chances of turning them into a living, because success has long depended partly on who can acquire expertise - through education, hiring, or knowing the right person to call. AI is making more of that expertise available on demand: a shop owner can analyze sales, build a storefront, and develop advertising without hiring three specialists, and a consultant can do work that once required junior staff. The episode asks what separates successful people when competent research, analysis, and execution become widely affordable - and what happens to people whose careers were built on selling expertise AI now distributes.
episodes.why: When AI hands everyone the analyst, programmer, and designer they could not afford, what is left to sell? A short, concrete take on expertise becoming on-demand.

episodes.title: [One Million AI Engineer Special] How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
episodes.about: What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year's homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford's CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course, and students have to learn an unfamiliar repo and propose a change. The episode is Latent Space's One Million AI Engineer special on how Stanford teaches AI-native engineering.
episodes.why: The long one: Stanford's CS146S had to be rebuilt because coding agents finish last year's homework in one prompt - maintainers now set the work, inside real open-source repos.
